Posted on November 26, 2026 by Jack Kelly

I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS. Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added new styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generator’s logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly.

To untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, “make the plan a value” or “decide what to do, and then do it”. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a “plan”, or a value of a “plan type”) describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

I really like this pattern because the “deciding what to do” part of a program is often more complicated than the “doing” part. Separating the two often turns the “deciding” part into a pure function that produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the “doing” phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), it’s more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing. (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a “dry run” printer or a “real” executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.)

This technique isn’t subtle or obscure. I’ve seen it called the plan-execute pattern, and the “routing slip” enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. I’ve previously called it a “tiny DSL”, and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article:

Often times, a simple non-recursive sum type “command” suffices as an interface between a pure function and an effectful one. A list of commands adds a lot of flexibility without dramatically complicating things.

Having resolved to introduce a plan type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record.

I found the generator’s logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern. The most complicated part of this change was response parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of ported response parsers, and a fall back to “do things the old way” for everything else:

-- | How to generate the parser for AWS's response to an API call.
data ResponseParser
  = -- | Perform no parsing and return an empty response. The response
    -- constructor in 'responseType' must take no arguments.
    ParseNull
  | -- | Parse the entire response as JSON.
    ParseAllJSON
  | -- | Parse the entire response as XML, with an optional wrapper.
    ParseAllXML (Maybe Text)
  | DoItTheOldWay

One thing that makes Amazonka’s generator rewarding to hack on is that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if there are no diffs and the generator doesn’t crash, the change probably didn’t break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled code relatively simple (not easy):

  1. If there are no unmigrated code paths, GOTO 9.
  2. Identify the least convoluted code path.
  3. Identify the service definitions that trigger it.
  4. Characterise the botocore feature that these service definitions rely on, and name it as a new constructor in ResponseParser.
  5. Replace the old code path with calls to error "whoops this is still live", so we crash if we try to use the old path.
  6. Regenerate all the AWS service bindings, and think harder if the generator throws the "whoops this is still live" error.
  7. If the generated bindings look the same, remove the dead code path and everything that it relied on (unused let bindings, parameters, etc.).
  8. GOTO 1.
  9. Remove the DoItTheOldWay shim constructors.

The end result worked well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring out status code parsing). Adding the idempotency machinery was then straightforward.

The data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more expressive plan types, such as “tiny DSLs”, “lists of commands”, or “free structures”. The trick is to keep a “do it the old way” constructor in your plan type until the “old way” has been refactored away.

A well-chosen plan type introduces a narrow waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the plan: things like testability, --dry-run, and simpler executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can also analyse and transform the plan itself. This is a great place to add pre-execution sanity checks or access controls. I regret that my tiny DSLs post inverted a transformation by interpreting it as matrix multiplications and inverting the result; it would have been simpler to provide an invert :: [Transform] -> [Transform] function.

Introducing alternate producers of the plan type can also pay off, but needs a bit more imagination:

  • Plans can be generated using a property testing library. This is an automatic and thorough way to explore the set of possible executions, and easier than trying to hand-craft pathological input cases.
  • Alternate front ends (such as a new CLI, a new API version, or a different request transport) can all be written against the same side-effectful core.
  • The completeness of a plan producer (e.g. an API version) can also be verified by property tests. Modern property testing libraries can declare coverage thresholds that fail if unmet, and so can ensure that every constructor of the plan type is reachable through the public interface.

“Making the plan a value” works well in any language, but Haskell’s laziness makes it especially nice. Lazy evaluation can avoid materialising the whole plan in memory if it is consumed right away. Even in strict languages, the decoupling benefits are great enough that the extra memory use is often worth it.
